questions.statement: What is the past simple form of the verb "arrive" for the pronoun "he"?
questions.context: The teacher writes a timeline on the board: Monday, arrival, meeting, departure.

options.text: arrives
options.feedback: Wrong. "Arrives" is the third person singular of the present simple, not the past simple.

options.text: arriving
options.feedback: Wrong. "Arriving" is the -ing form used in continuous tenses, not the past simple.

options.text: was arrived
options.feedback: Wrong. "Was arrived" is not used in English; the passive would be "was arrived at", but the active past simple is simply "arrived".

options.text: arrived
options.feedback: Correct. The past simple of "to arrive" for he or she is "arrived", formed by adding -ed to the base form.

questions.explanation: Regular verbs form the past simple with -ed after the base form, while irregular verbs change their form entirely, as in "go" to "went".
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which option completes the sentence correctly?
questions.context: Maria says: "I ___ to San Salvador last Saturday with my cousin."

options.text: went
options.feedback: Correct. The sentence talks about a finished action in the past, and "go" is irregular, so its past simple is "went".

options.text: go
options.feedback: Wrong. "Go" is the base form, which cannot follow the past auxiliary "did" or stand alone for a past action.

options.text: gone
options.feedback: Wrong. "Gone" is the past participle used after "have" or "has", not the past simple.

options.text: going
options.feedback: Wrong. "Going" is the -ing form and needs "was" or "were" before it.

questions.explanation: When the verb is irregular, only the middle form changes: go becomes went in the past simple and gone in the past participle.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What correction does the teacher need to make?
questions.context: A student writes: "Yesterday I buyed a new backpack at the market."

options.text: "Buyed" is correct because all verbs add -ed
options.feedback: Wrong. Only regular verbs take -ed; irregular ones change form and "buy" is one of them.

options.text: "Buyed" must be "bought", because "buy" is an irregular verb
options.feedback: Correct. "Buy" is irregular, so its past simple is "bought" and not "buyed".

options.text: The word "yesterday" must be removed
options.feedback: Wrong. "Yesterday" is a correct marker of past time and is exactly what the sentence needs.

options.text: "Buyed" should be "buys" because the subject is "I"
options.feedback: Wrong. "Buys" belongs to the third person singular present simple, which does not match the past time marker.

questions.explanation: Irregular verbs such as buy, break and choose form the past simple without -ed, so the student must learn them as whole words.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is wrong with the sentence?
questions.context: The sentence reads: "He didn't went to the party last night."

options.text: "Didn't" should be "doesn't"
options.feedback: Wrong. "Doesn't" is present simple; the sentence has the past time marker "last night", so "didn't" is right.

options.text: After the auxiliary "did", the main verb must be in its base form
options.feedback: Correct. "Didn't" already carries the past tense, so the verb after it stays in the base form: "didn't go".

options.text: "Went" should be "gone"
options.feedback: Wrong. "Gone" needs "have" or "has" before it and does not follow "did".

options.text: Nothing is wrong; the sentence is correct
options.feedback: Wrong. Using a past form after "did" is a double marking of the tense and is incorrect in standard English.

questions.explanation: The auxiliary already carries the tense and the negative, so the main verb returns to the base form after "did", "does" and "do".
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which time connector best links the last completed action in that sequence?
questions.context: A student wants to describe a sequence of three past actions in a story.

options.text: yet
options.feedback: Wrong. "Yet" is mainly used in questions and negatives, and it does not mark the next step of a past sequence.

options.text: since
options.feedback: Wrong. "Since" marks a starting point in time, not the order of events in a past narrative.

options.text: then
options.feedback: Correct. "Then" introduces the next step in a sequence of past events and keeps the narration in the past simple.

options.text: while
options.feedback: Wrong. "While" introduces a contrast or a simultaneous action, not a successive step.

questions.explanation: In a past narrative, "first", "then", "after that" and "finally" mark the order of the events as they happened.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the past simple of "study" and "cry"?
questions.context: The class reviews the spelling of past simple forms that end in a consonant plus y.

options.text: studyed and cryed
options.feedback: Wrong. English does not keep the y when adding -ed after a consonant; the y must change to i.

options.text: studied and cryed
options.feedback: Wrong. The rule applies to both verbs, so the second form must also be "cried" with i.

options.text: studied and cried
options.feedback: Correct. With a consonant plus y the y changes to i before -ed, giving "studied" and "cried".

options.text: studiyed and criyed
options.feedback: Wrong. No extra syllable is inserted; only the letter y changes to i before the -ed ending.

questions.explanation: Spelling rules for the past simple: consonant plus y changes to i, as in study to studied, while vowel plus y just adds -ed, as in play to played.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence uses the past simple correctly?
questions.context: A student must write about what happened during the summer holiday.

options.text: We visit the beach and we swam in the ocean
options.feedback: Wrong. "Visit" is present simple, so the tense is inconsistent with the past time marker.

options.text: We visited the beach and we swim in the ocean
options.feedback: Wrong. "Swim" is present simple and does not match the past action being narrated.

options.text: We will visit the beach and we swam in the ocean
options.feedback: Wrong. "Will" points to the future, and the holiday this sentence refers to is already over.

options.text: We visited the beach and we swam in the ocean
options.feedback: Correct. Both "visited" and "swam" are past simple forms, so the whole sentence is in the past.

questions.explanation: When several actions in one sentence belong to the same past period, all of them take the past simple form.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the error in that sentence?
questions.context: The teacher writes: "She wrote three emails and she was send them to her boss."

options.text: "Was send" is correct because the subject is singular
options.feedback: Wrong. The singular subject is right for "was", but the participle "send" is not a past participle.

options.text: "Wrote" should be "written"
options.feedback: Wrong. "Written" is the participle and would need "has" or "had" before it.

options.text: "Was send" is wrong; the past passive needs "were sent"
options.feedback: Correct. In the past passive the auxiliary is "were" for plural subjects, and the participle is "sent".

options.text: There is no error in the sentence
options.feedback: Wrong. "Was send" mixes the auxiliary "was" with a base form instead of a participle.

questions.explanation: In the past passive the pattern is "was" or "were" plus the past participle, and the participle of "send" is "sent".
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which statement correctly distinguishes the two tenses?
questions.context: Two students disagree about the difference between the past simple and the present perfect.

options.text: Both tenses refer to unfinished actions in the past
options.feedback: Wrong. The past simple always presents the action as finished and located in the past.

options.text: The present perfect cannot be used with words of time
options.feedback: Wrong. The present perfect is frequently used with time expressions like "today", "this week" or "already".

options.text: The past simple is only used with the verb "to be"
options.feedback: Wrong. The past simple covers regular and irregular action verbs as well as "to be".

options.text: The past simple refers to a finished action at a definite past time; the present perfect links a past action to the present
options.feedback: Correct. A specific past time such as "yesterday" goes with the past simple, while "already" or "this year" go with the present perfect.

questions.explanation: The past simple needs a finished past moment, while the present perfect uses that past action to say something about now.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which option makes the negative sentence correct?
questions.context: A student writes: "She didn't went to school because she was sick."

options.text: She didn't go to school because she was sick
options.feedback: Correct. After "didn't" the verb returns to its base form "go".

options.text: She didn't went to school because she was sick
options.feedback: Wrong. "Went" is the past form and cannot follow the negative auxiliary "didn't".

options.text: She not didn't go to school because she was sick
options.feedback: Wrong. After "did" the negative must be formed with "not", and "didn't" already includes that negation.

options.text: She doesn't went to school because she was sick
options.feedback: Wrong. "Doesn't" is present simple and cannot be combined with the past form "went".

questions.explanation: The negative past simple is built with "did not" or "didn't" followed by the base form of the main verb.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the phrase "By 2010" signal in that passage?
questions.context: The reading passage says: "In 1998, the company opened two factories. By 2010, it had opened twenty."

options.text: A completed point in time by which the action was finished
options.feedback: Correct. "By" plus a past time marks the end of a period up to which the action had already happened.

options.text: A repeated habit in the past
options.feedback: Wrong. A repeated past habit would need "used to" or "every year", not "by".

options.text: An action that is still happening now
options.feedback: Wrong. The action is presented as finished, since the twenty factories had already been opened.

options.text: A future event planned for 2010
options.feedback: Wrong. Everything in the passage is in the past; "by 2010" looks back, not forward.

questions.explanation: Expressions such as "by the end of 2010" or "by then" mark the deadline before which an action was completed.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence reports those actions in the past simple?
questions.context: A student wants to report a completed sequence of actions from a work shift.

options.text: I check the order, I pack the boxes and I called the client
options.feedback: Wrong. "Check" and "pack" are present simple, so the sequence mixes tenses.

options.text: I checked the order, I packed the boxes and I called the client
options.feedback: Correct. All three verbs take the past simple, which is what a sequence of completed actions requires.

options.text: I am checking the order, I packed the boxes and I call the client
options.feedback: Wrong. The present continuous and the present simple do not belong in a report of completed actions.

options.text: I have checked the order, I pack the boxes and I called the client
options.feedback: Wrong. "Have checked" links to the present, while the rest of the sentence narrates the past.

questions.explanation: When a speaker reports what was done during a finished period, every action in the list takes the past simple.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the past simple of the verb "buy"?
questions.context: The teacher shows a list of irregular verbs and asks the class to complete the past simple column.

options.text: buyed
options.feedback: Wrong. Adding -ed is only for regular verbs; "buy" does not follow that pattern.

options.text: buy
options.feedback: Wrong. The base form also fails, since a finished past action needs a past form and not the infinitive.

options.text: bought
options.feedback: Correct. "Buy" is irregular and its past simple is "bought".

options.text: buying
options.feedback: Wrong. "Buying" needs "was" or "were" before it and belongs to the continuous forms.

questions.explanation: Common irregular verbs in the past simple include buy to bought, bring to brought, teach to taught and catch to caught.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Why does the reporter use the past simple in both sentences?
questions.context: A newspaper report reads: "The hurricane struck the coast at midnight. Thousands of families left their homes that night."

options.text: To show that the hurricane is still happening
options.feedback: Wrong. The past simple presents the action as finished, not as ongoing.

options.text: To compare the two events in duration
options.feedback: Wrong. Comparing duration would need comparative forms such as "longer" or "for two hours".

options.text: To express doubt about the events
options.feedback: Wrong. Doubt is expressed with modals or hedging, not by the choice of tense.

options.text: To report events that happened and are finished at a definite time
options.feedback: Correct. A news report about completed events uses the past simple to locate them in a closed past period.

questions.explanation: The past simple is the default tense for reporting completed news events with a closed time reference.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which opening sentence suits a plot summary best?
questions.context: A student must summarise a movie plot for a class presentation.

options.text: The film is telling the story of a family that is moving to the coast
options.feedback: Wrong. The present continuous would suggest the story is happening now, which is not the case.

options.text: The film tells the story of a family that moved to the coast and faced many problems
options.feedback: Correct. The past simple is the standard tense for narrating the events of a completed story.

options.text: The film has been telling the story of a family that moved to the coast
options.feedback: Wrong. The present perfect would link the story to the present, but a finished plot is normally narrated in the past.

options.text: The film tells the story of a family that will move to the coast
options.feedback: Wrong. "Will" refers to the future, but the plot of a film has already been narrated.

questions.explanation: A completed narrative, whether real or fictional, is normally told in the past simple.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the reason?
questions.context: The teacher asks why the student cannot say "He have finished the report yesterday."

options.text: The present perfect is never used with "yesterday"
options.feedback: Wrong. The point is not that "yesterday" is forbidden, but that stating a finished past time forces the past simple.

options.text: A definite past time such as "yesterday" requires the past simple, not the present perfect
options.feedback: Correct. When the past time is stated, English uses the past simple and not the present perfect.

options.text: "Have" should be "has" because the subject is "he"
options.feedback: Wrong. The subject does agree with "has", but the real problem is the use of the present perfect.

options.text: The sentence is correct and only the spelling is wrong
options.feedback: Wrong. This is a grammar pattern problem, not an orthography problem.

questions.explanation: The present perfect is not used with finished past time expressions such as "yesterday", "last week" or "in 2020".
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which correction should the student make?
questions.context: A student is asked to correct the sentence "They was late for the exam."

options.text: They was late for the exam
options.feedback: Wrong. "Was" is the singular past form and does not agree with the plural subject "they".

options.text: They are late for the exam
options.feedback: Wrong. "Are" is present simple, but the exam has already taken place.

options.text: They were late for the exam
options.feedback: Correct. The subject "they" is plural, so the past simple of "to be" is "were".

options.text: They will be late for the exam
options.feedback: Wrong. "Will" points to the future, but the exam has already taken place.

questions.explanation: The verb "to be" is irregular: in the past simple it is "was" for singular subjects and "were" for plural ones.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What do all of those expressions have in common?
questions.context: The teacher gives the class a list of time expressions: yesterday, last night, two days ago, in 2019.

options.text: They all point to a finished moment in the past, so they go with the past simple
options.feedback: Correct. A finished past time reference requires the past simple, not the present perfect.

options.text: They all point to a moment that is still happening
options.feedback: Wrong. Every expression on the list refers to a time that has already ended.

options.text: They can all be used with the present perfect
options.feedback: Wrong. A finished past time rules out the present perfect.

options.text: They all refer to future events
options.feedback: Wrong. None of these expressions points forward in time.

questions.explanation: Finished time expressions such as "yesterday" or "in 2019" are incompatible with the present perfect, which needs an unfinished or unspecified past period.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence mixes the past and the future correctly?
questions.context: A student is writing a short message about a weekend activity and wants to ask a friend to join next time.

options.text: We visited the market yesterday, so we can go again next Saturday
options.feedback: Correct. The first clause reports a finished past action and the second uses "can" for the future possibility.

options.text: We visited the market yesterday, so we can go yesterday
options.feedback: Wrong. "Yesterday" cannot be repeated as a future time; the second action needs a future expression.

options.text: We visit the market yesterday, so we can go again next Saturday
options.feedback: Wrong. "Visit" is present simple, but "yesterday" requires a past form.

options.text: We visited the market yesterday, so we went again next Saturday
options.feedback: Wrong. "Went again" is past, but "next Saturday" is still in the future from the speaker's point of view.

questions.explanation: In a single sentence the tense follows the time reference of each clause, not the tense of the neighbouring clause.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which verb follows that pattern?
questions.context: The class is building a list of verbs whose past simple ends in -d even though the base form does not.

options.text: work
options.feedback: Wrong. "Work" is regular and takes -ed, giving "worked".

options.text: play
options.feedback: Wrong. "Play" is regular and takes -ed, giving "played".

options.text: open
options.feedback: Wrong. "Open" is regular and takes -ed, giving "opened".

options.text: send
options.feedback: Correct. "Send" ends in -d already, and its past simple is the single-syllable form "sent".

questions.explanation: Irregular verbs whose past simple does not take -ed include send to sent, make to made, tell to told and buy to bought.
questions.subject: ingles
